question: What is the meaning of customer requirements in relation to customer  information?
description: Customer requirements in relation to customer information refer to the need for transparency, data privacy, portability, and access longevity. These requirements are essential for consumers to have trustworthy data exchange, maintain security, confidentiality, and intellectual property (IP) protection. They also ensure that data is accessible, interoperable, and traceable, which is crucial for the development of the Digital Product Passport (DPP). The customer requirements for the information included in the DPP are analyzed in several studies, highlighting the importance of these dimensions for a solid regulatory framework.

The need for a solid regulatory framework is particularly relevant and can be identified in 11 studies [2], [45], [39], 
[48], [22], [32], [5], [38], [20], [24], [35], followed by the real-time availability of product information [32], [38], 
[20], [24], [35], [10]. Requirements for the information included in DPP are analyzed in five works [39], [5], [24], 
[35], [10]. Product sustainability, circularity performance [2], [5], [24], [35], functional suitability [2], [32], [38], [20], 
and value chain actor information [45], [22], [5], [35] are of the utmost importance to consumers while maintaining 
security, confidentiality, and intellectual property (IP) protection [39], [22], [32], [20]. Data requirements include 
accessibility [32], [20], [24], [10], interoperability [32], [20], [24], modularity and modifiability (e.g., change in one 
component has minimal impact on another) [32], [38], [20], traceability [5], [24], [35] and communication/sharing 
information [24], [35], [15]. Finally, the requirements of transparency [5], [31], data privacy [32], [20], portability 
[32], [20], access longevity [24], and third-party verification [24] were also mentioned. 
These requirements address interrelated dimensions of (1) mandatory/voluntary regulations (e.g., privacy, IP 
protection, verification), (2) data since the early stages of data identification and collection, preferably with IoT, 
including sharing and retention over time, (3) business-related (e.g., transparency, value chain iterations, and 
availability), and (4) technical (e.g., cybersecurity, modules, interoperability standards). However, they seem to 
uncover only the top of the iceberg when we consider the voluntary disclosure of information and use of the DPP, for 
example, to provide valuable data for AI approaches, namely, supplier product selection based on DPP data and final 
product requirements, benchmarking and alternative product classification, or prediction of combined circularity 
potential within complex supply chains. The next section summarizes the challenges in the four main types of 
requirements.
